Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is a severe disease caused by the ascomycete fungus Venturia inaequalis. It attacks leaves, petioles, blossoms, and fruit, resulting in olive-green to black velvety spots and deformed fruit.
symptoms: Dull olive-green to brown velvety lesions on upper leaf surfaces
Curling and distortion of young developing leaves
Premature leaf yellowing and early defoliation
Scabby, corky dark spots on apple fruit that crack as fruit expands
causes: Fungal pathogen Venturia inaequalis
Overwintering in fallen dead leaves on orchard floor
Prolonged leaf wetness (6-9+ hours) during cool spring rains (12-24°C)

organic: Apply sulfur-based fungicides or liquid lime sulfur during early bud break
Foliar spray of Potassium Bicarbonate during active spore discharge
Bio-fungicide drench using Bacillus subtilis strains
chemical: Captan 50 WP (2-2.5 kg/ha) at pink bud and petal fall stages
Myclobutanil or Difenoconazole for systemic curative control
Mancozeb 75 WP as protective spring canopy cover
cultural: Rake and destroy or chop fallen infected orchard leaves in autumn
Apply urea 5% spray to fallen leaves before winter to speed decomposition
Prune inner canopy branches to enhance sunlight penetration and wind drying

prevention: Plant scab-resistant cultivars (e.g., Liberty, Enterprise, Freedom, Prima)
Maintain wide tree spacing to maximize air circulation
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; employ under-canopy micro-drip
references: Cornell University Cooperative Extension - Tree Fruit Pathology
UC Davis IPM - Apple Scab Management Guidelines

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot is caused by the fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa. It affects apple fruit, leaves (known as frogeye leaf spot), and wood cankers, causing firm brown rot on fruit that mummifies.
symptoms: Small purple leaf spots that enlarge into circular lesions with tan centers (frogeye appearance)
Firm brown rotting zones on fruit starting near the calyx end
Concentric dark and light rings on expanding fruit rot
Sunken limb cankers with bark cracking and black pycnidia pustules
causes: Fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa
Overwinters in dead mummified fruit, dead twigs, and fire blight cankers
Spore dispersal driven by warm rain (20-27°C)

organic: Copper octanoate or Bordeaux mixture at dormant bud break
Bio-fungicide applications of Trichoderma harzianum to wound cuts
chemical: Captan or Thiophanate-methyl foliar sprays beginning at silver tip
Flint (Trifloxystrobin) applied in petal fall cover sprays
cultural: Prune out dead wood, cankered branches, and fire blight blighted shoots
Remove and incinerate all hanging mummified apples before bud swelling
Burn or discard all pruned wood away from the orchard

prevention: Protect trees against fire blight, winter freeze injury, and hail damage
Maintain vigorous tree nutrition without excessive late-summer nitrogen
references: Penn State Extension - Apple Diseases: Black Rot
Purdue Extension - Fruit Disease Management

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar apple rust is caused by the heteroecious rust fungus Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae. It requires two host plants: apple/crabapple and eastern red cedar/juniper to complete its two-year life cycle.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange or reddish circular spots on upper apple leaf surface
Raised orange pustules with black pycnial dots in the center
Small tube-like projections (aecia) on the underside of infected leaves
Premature leaf dropping and distorted fruit blemishes
causes: Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae rust fungus
Proximity to infected Juniper/Red Cedar trees harboring galls
Wind-blown basidiospores during wet spring weather (10-24°C)

organic: Sulfur dust or wettable sulfur applied before forecasted spring rain events
Serenade (Bacillus subtilis) preventive leaf spray
chemical: Myclobutanil (Immunox) applied from pink bud through early summer
Mancozeb or Propiconazole applied on 7-10 day protective schedule
cultural: Remove nearby Eastern Red Cedar and ornamental junipers within 1-2 miles if feasible
Hand-prune cedar galls (brown woody swellings) from nearby ornamental junipers during winter

prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties (e.g., Enterprise, Liberty, Redfree, Freedom)
Scout cedar hosts in late winter before gelatinous orange telial horns erupt
references: University of Minnesota Extension - Cedar Apple Rust
Virginia Tech Extension - Gymnosporangium Rusts

Apple___healthy.description: The apple foliage demonstrates uniform dark green pigmentation, intact cuticle, robust vein architecture, and absence of fungal or bacterial lesions.
symptoms: Uniform rich green color across leaf blade
Unblemished leaf margin with smooth or finely serrated edges
Normal leaf expansion without cupping, chlorosis, or necrotic spots

organic: Continue regular compost tea foliar drenches and balanced micronutrient nutrition
chemical: No chemical intervention required
cultural: Maintain balanced orchard irrigation and clean canopy sanitation

prevention: Maintain regular monitoring traps for codling moth and apple maggot
Conduct annual soil and leaf tissue testing to ensure balanced potassium and boron
references: USDA Agricultural Research Service - Orchard Health Standards

Blueberry___healthy.description: Vibrant, healthy highbush or rabbiteye blueberry leaves with uniform green pigmentation, smooth glossy surface, and no signs of leaf scorch, rust, or mummy berry.
symptoms: Glossy, dark green elliptical foliage
Sturdy petiole attachments without shoot dieback
No interveinal chlorosis or fungal spots

organic: Maintain acidic organic pine bark mulch layer (5-10 cm) around root zone
chemical: No chemical treatment required
cultural: Maintain drip irrigation and ensure soil pH remains between 4.5 and 5.2

prevention: Monitor soil acidity regularly with elemental sulfur additions as needed
Prune older canes (over 5-6 years) during winter dormancy to stimulate young vigorous canes
references: Michigan State University Extension - Blueberry Production Guide

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.description: Caused by Podosphaera clandestina, powdery mildew attacks young expanding cherry leaves and developing fruit, causing curled leaves and a white talcum powder-like fungal coating.
symptoms: White powdery fungal patches on lower leaf surface expanding to upper surface
Leaves cup upward, crinkle, and exhibit distorted growth
Young terminal shoots become stunted and distorted
Mature leaves develop yellowish chlorotic areas
causes: Podosphaera clandestina fungus
Overwintering as cleistothecia in bark crevices and orchard litter
Warm days (15-27°C) combined with high relative humidity and overcast skies

organic: Apply potassium bicarbonate (3-5 g/liter) or horticultural oil spray (1-2%)
Wettable sulfur applied before bloom and at petal fall
chemical: Quinoxyfen, Myclobutanil, or Trifloxystrobin applied at shuck fall and cover sprays
Rotate FRAC groups to prevent fungicide resistance development
cultural: Prune dense canopy water sprouts to allow thorough air circulation and sunlight
Avoid high nitrogen fertilizer applications which promote susceptible young flush

prevention: Plant mildew-tolerant cherry rootstocks and scions where adapted
Apply preventive sprays during early post-shuck fall when young fruit is vulnerable
references: Washington State University Extension - Cherry Powdery Mildew Management
UC IPM Pest Management Guidelines - Cherries

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.description: Healthy sweet or sour cherry leaves displaying vigorous deep-green coloring, erect petioles, and complete freedom from shot-hole disease, powdery mildew, or bacterial canker.
symptoms: Glossy dark green leaves with clean serrated margins
Vigorous shoot extension without terminal wilting
Absence of necrotic perforations (shot-holes) or leaf spots

organic: Continue foliar kelp extract spray during fruit sizing
chemical: No chemical treatment required
cultural: Ensure consistent drip moisture during fruit swell

prevention: Apply preventive copper wash at late autumn leaf drop to protect leaf scars from bacterial canker
references: Oregon State University Extension - Cherry Orchard Guide

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: Gray leaf spot is caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis. It is one of the most destructive corn foliar diseases worldwide, causing rectangular necrotic lesions that run parallel to leaf veins.
symptoms: Small tan spots with yellow halos that expand into long rectangular lesions
Lesions strictly delimited by parallel leaf veins (blocky rectangular shape)
Lesions turn grayish as fungus sporulates under high humidity
Extensive leaf blighting and premature plant senescence causing stalk lodging
causes: Cercospora zeae-maydis fungal pathogen
High corn-on-corn residue from minimum or no-till cropping systems
Prolonged warm, humid weather (24-32°C and >90% humidity for 12+ hours)

organic: Bio-fungicides based on Bacillus amyloliquefaciens applied at early tassel
Copper hydroxide sprays for smallholder plots
chemical: Strobilurin and triazole premixes (e.g., Azoxystrobin + Difenoconazole)
Pyraclostrobin + Fluxapyroxad applied at V12 to VT (tasseling) stage
Apply chemical control if lesions appear on third leaf below ear before tasseling
cultural: Rotate with non-host crops such as soybeans, wheat, or alfalfa for 1-2 years
Shred and incorporate crop residue into the soil to accelerate decomposition

prevention: Plant hybrid corn with high genetic resistance ratings to Gray Leaf Spot
Avoid planting at excessively high plant densities in low-lying fog-prone fields
references: Purdue University Extension - Gray Leaf Spot of Corn
Iowa State University - Crop Protection Network: Corn Diseases

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Common rust is caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi. It produces powdery reddish-brown pustules scattered across both upper and lower leaf surfaces, reducing photosynthetically active leaf area.
symptoms: Golden-brown to cinnamon-brown powdery pustules (uredinia) on upper and lower surfaces
Pustules are circular to elongate and rupture leaf epidermis easily
Pustules turn brownish-black late in the season as dark teliospores form
Severe infections result in leaf chlorosis, death, and poor ear filling
causes: Fungal obligate parasite Puccinia sorghi
Windborne spores carried northwards on weather fronts from southern production regions
Moderate temperatures (16-25°C) combined with high relative humidity (near 100%) and dew

organic: Sulfur dust applications on young sweet corn
Neem seed kernel extract foliar wash
chemical: Triazole fungicides (Propiconazole, Tebuconazole) applied when 6+ pustules per leaf appear before tasseling
Strobilurin fungicides (Azoxystrobin, Pyraclostrobin)
cultural: Early planting to avoid peak midsummer spore showers
Balanced balanced potassium fertilization to increase stalk strength

prevention: Select sweet corn and field corn hybrids possessing Rp gene resistance
Monitor fields weekly starting at vegetative V6 stage
references: University of Illinois Extension - Common Rust of Corn
University of Minnesota Extension - Corn Rust Management

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern corn leaf blight (NCLB) is caused by Exserohilum turcicum. It causes large, cigar-shaped grayish-green to tan lesions that can coalesce and burn entire leaf canopies.
symptoms: Large elliptical, cigar-shaped lesions (2.5 to 15 cm long) on leaves
Lesions start grayish-green, drying to tan or brown
Dark olive-green sooty fungal sporulation inside lesions in damp morning weather
Premature canopy desiccation and reduced grain weight
causes: Fungus Exserohilum turcicum (Setosphaeria turcica)
Overwintering in unburied corn debris
Extended dew periods (6-8 hours) and moderate temperatures (18-27°C)

organic: Bacillus subtilis foliar bio-fungicide sprays
Copper-based protective sprays
chemical: Pyraclostrobin + Metconazole or Azoxystrobin + Propiconazole applied between V14 and R1
Apply when lesions are established on leaves below ear level prior to silking
cultural: Tillage to bury corn residue below soil surface in high-incidence zones
Minimum 1-year crop rotation out of corn

prevention: Select corn hybrids containing Ht-resistance genes (Ht1, Ht2, Ht3, or HtN)
Ensure adequate balanced phosphorus and potassium nutrition
references: Ohio State University Extension - Northern Corn Leaf Blight
CGIAR / CIMMYT - Maize Doctor Diagnostic Guide

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: Healthy corn leaves showing clean parallel venation, rich dark green chlorophyll pigmentation, and robust sheath attachment without fungal pustules or blights.
symptoms: Uniform green leaf blade with intact midrib
Absence of rectangular, circular, or cigar-shaped lesions
Vigorous photosynthetic canopy with healthy leaf angle

organic: Apply balanced nitrogen side-dressing via organic blood meal or compost manure
chemical: No chemical treatment required
cultural: Maintain clean weed-free cultivation and optimal plant population

prevention: Scout for western corn rootworm and corn borer pests regularly
Soil testing to maintain optimum nitrogen, zinc, and magnesium levels
references: Purdue University Corn Extension Guide

Grape___Black_rot.description: Grape black rot is caused by Guignardia bidwellii. It is a highly destructive fungal disease in warm, humid regions that blights leaves and turns berries into hard, shriveled black mummies.
symptoms: Small circular reddish-brown leaf spots with dark margins and tiny black pycnidia pimples
Infected berries turn pale brown, shrivel rapidly, and transform into hard black wrinkled mummies
Elongated dark cankers on shoots and tendrils
causes: Fungus Guignardia bidwellii
Overwintering in mummified berries hanging on vines or fallen on vineyard floor
Rain-splashed ascospores and conidia during warm humid spring weather (21-27°C)

organic: Copper hydroxide or Bordeaux mixture applied at early shoot growth (7-10 cm)
Lime sulfur applied during delayed dormant stage
chemical: Myclobutanil (Rally 40WSP) or Tebuconazole applied from pre-bloom through 4 weeks post-bloom
Mancozeb or Ziram applied as protectant before critical bloom rain events
cultural: Flail mow or till vineyard floor in early spring to bury overwintered mummies
Canopy shoot thinning and leaf pulling around fruit zone to maximize drying
Prune out and destroy infected cane lesions during winter pruning

prevention: Ensure open trellis design (VSP or high wire cordon) for optimum ventilation
Critical protective window is from immediate pre-bloom until 4-5 weeks after cap fall
references: Cornell University - Grape Black Rot Management
Penn State Extension - Grape Disease Management

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: Esca is a complex grapevine trunk disease caused by a succession of wood-inhabiting fungi including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Fomitiporia mediterranea, causing tiger-stripe leaf patterns and berry speckling.
symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' chlorotic and necrotic patterns between leaf veins
Small dark brown to purple spots on berry skins ('black measles')
Berry cracking and drying on clusters
Sudden summer apoplexy (complete vine collapse and wilting within days)
causes: Complex of fungal wood decay pathogens (Phaeomoniella, Phaeoacremonium, Fomitiporia)
Infection through large pruning wounds during wet winter weather
Vascular vessel occlusion and toxic fungal metabolites

organic: Trichoderma-based pruning wound sealants (e.g., Esquive, Vintec)
Remedial surgery: cut out trunk wood cankers 10 cm below infected zone
chemical: Paint large winter pruning cuts immediately with Topsin-M (Thiophanate-methyl) or acrylic paste
There are no effective curative systemic fungicides once inside heartwood
cultural: Delay winter pruning until late winter/early spring when wound healing is rapid
Double pruning technique: pre-prune early, final prune close to bud break
Disinfect pruning shears regularly with 70% alcohol or bleach solution

prevention: Purchase certified disease-free grafted grape nursery rootstocks
Avoid creating large pruning wounds in moist rainfall conditions
references: UC Davis IPM - Grape Esca (Black Measles)
OIV (International Organisation of Vine and Wine) - Grapevine Trunk Diseases

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: Grape leaf blight is caused by Phaeoisariopsis vitis (Isariopsis clavispora). It creates irregular brown spots that coalesce, causing premature leaf yellowing and defoliation late in the season.
symptoms: Irregular, angular reddish-brown to dark brown spots on mature leaves
Lesions show a darker boundary and olive-brown velvety sporulation on underside
Severe infections trigger premature leaf drop before harvest
Incomplete berry maturation due to loss of photosynthetic leaf canopy
causes: Fungus Phaeoisariopsis vitis
Overwintering in fallen grape leaf debris and dormant canes
Warm, wet, humid late-summer conditions with frequent rain or dew

organic: Copper oxychloride or Bordeaux mixture applied after fruit set
Sulfur sprays applied on 10-14 day intervals
chemical: Mancozeb 75 WP or Chlorothalonil applied post-bloom
Kresoxim-methyl or Pyraclostrobin during active canopy development
cultural: Rake, destroy, or compost fallen autumn foliage away from vineyard
Prune canopy for adequate aeration and sun penetration to foliage

prevention: Maintain balanced canopy density without dense inner clusters
Avoid overhead irrigation systems
references: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension - Grape Disease Handbook
ICAR - National Research Centre for Grapes (India)

Grape___healthy.description: Vigorous grapevine foliage displaying uniform green coloration, intact palmate lobe leaf structure, healthy petioles, and robust tendril growth with zero signs of mildew, rots, or trunk disease.
symptoms: Lush green palmate leaves with healthy serrations
No powdery white coatings, black spots, or interveinal yellowing
Active cane elongation with healthy tendrils

organic: Apply balanced potassium and magnesium foliar feeds
chemical: No chemical treatments needed
cultural: Maintain canopy wire tucking and summer shoot hedging

prevention: Regular scouting for grapevine leafhopper and grapevine moth
Annual petiole analysis at bloom to manage vineyard nutrient balance
references: UC Davis Viticulture Extension - Healthy Vine Guidelines

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: Huanglongbing (HLB) or Citrus Greening is an incurable, devastating disease caused by the phloem-restricted bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, vectored by the Asian citrus psyllid (Diaphorina citri).
symptoms: Asymmetrical blotchy mottle leaf yellowing across veins (not matching on both leaf halves)
Yellowing of individual shoot sectors ('yellow shoots')
Raised, corky, thickened leaf veins with upright 'rabbit-ear' leaf angle
Small, lopsided, bitter fruit that stays green at the blossom end ('greening')
causes: Bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus (CLas)
Transmitted by the Asian Citrus Psyllid (Diaphorina citri)
Graft transmission from infected budwood

organic: Spray horticultural mineral oils or neem oil to suppress psyllid nymphs
Release biological control agents such as Tamarixia radiata parasitoid wasps
Nutritional foliar sprays (zinc, manganese, boron) to prolong tree productivity
chemical: Systemic insecticides (Imidacloprid, Thiamethoxam) to suppress vector psyllid populations
Trunk injection of oxytetracycline (where legally approved for bearing trees)
No cure exists for infected trees; prompt tree removal is standard protocol
cultural: Aggressive scout-and-scramble: identify and immediately remove symptomatic trees
Control surrounding Murraya paniculata (orange jasmine) ornamental host plants

prevention: Strictly plant certified disease-free nursery stock grown in insect-proof screenhouses
Establish regional psyllid management coordinated spray zones
Quarantine enforcement: never move uncertified citrus plants or cuttings
references: University of Florida IFAS Extension - Citrus Greening (HLB)
USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) - Citrus Health

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot of peach is caused by Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. It attacks leaves, twigs, and fruit, causing angular purplish-brown leaf lesions with 'shot-hole' drop-out and fruit pitting.
symptoms: Small angular water-soaked purple-brown spots near leaf tips and midribs
Dead centers of lesions drop out giving a shot-hole appearance
Severe leaf yellowing followed by defoliation
Deep, pitted, cracked lesions on peach fruit that exude gum during wet weather
causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni
Overwinters in twig cankers and terminal bud scales
Windblown rain, sand abrasion, and warm spring temperatures (21-29°C)

organic: Copper bactericide applications during dormant season up to delayed dormant
Cueva (copper octanoate) at low rates during early foliage development
chemical: Oxytetracycline (Mycoshield) applied weekly starting from petal fall to shuck split
Low-rate copper hydroxide sprays rotated with antibiotics
cultural: Prune out infected twig cankers during dry winter weather
Avoid high nitrogen applications that create succulent late growth

prevention: Plant resistant peach varieties (e.g., Candor, Clayton, Redhaven, Biscoe)
Plant windbreaks on sandy soils to prevent abrasive windblown sand damage
references: Clemson University Cooperative Extension - Peach Bacterial Spot
Penn State Extension - Tree Fruit Production Guide

Peach___healthy.description: Healthy peach tree leaves showing glossy lanceolate leaves, bright green color, clean margins, and total absence of leaf curl, shot-holes, or bacterial canker gumming.
symptoms: Smooth, lanceolate leaves with finely serrated borders
Vibrant green pigmentation without puckering or purpling
Intact petioles with healthy glands at base

organic: Apply balanced organic orchard mulch and seaweed foliar spray
chemical: No chemical treatment required
cultural: Maintain summer fruit thinning and open-center canopy architecture

prevention: Apply single dormant copper spray at autumn leaf fall to prevent peach leaf curl (Taphrina deformans)
references: UC Davis IPM - Peach Disease Management

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria. It is one of the most devastating pepper diseases, producing circular to irregular water-soaked spots, defoliation, and fruit blistering.
symptoms: Small circular water-soaked lesions that turn dark brown with pale centers
Lesions prominent on lower leaf surfaces with rough brown texture
Severe chlorosis and extensive leaf drop exposing fruit to sunscald
Rough, circular raised scabby warts on pepper fruit surface
causes: Bacterium Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria
Contaminated seed or infected transplant seedlings
Warm temperatures (24-30°C) with rain splashes, dew, or overhead sprinklers

organic: Fixed copper bactericide (copper hydroxide) combined with bio-fungicides (Bacillus subtilis)
Foliar spray of bacteriophages specific to Xanthomonas (AgriPhage)
chemical: Copper hydroxide tank-mixed with Mancozeb for improved bactericidal efficacy
Actigard (Acibenzolar-S-methyl) plant defense activator applied preventively
cultural: Strictly avoid overhead irrigation; use under-mulch drip lines
Do not work in pepper fields while foliage is wet
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops (corn, beans, brassicas) for minimum 2 years

prevention: Use certified pathogen-free, hot-water treated pepper seeds (50°C for 25 min)
Plant bell pepper hybrids possessing multi-race bacterial spot resistance (X10R varieties)
references: University of Florida IFAS Extension - Bacterial Spot of Pepper
Cornell Vegetable Program - Pepper Disease Management

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: Healthy bell pepper foliage displaying deep green, glossy ovate leaves with smooth margins, sturdy stems, and no signs of bacterial spot, anthracnose, or viral mosaic mottling.
symptoms: Lush dark green ovate leaves
Firm upright canopy with robust flowering nodes
Absence of necrotic specks, chlorotic halos, or leaf curling

organic: Apply balanced calcium-magnesium foliar spray to prevent blossom end rot
chemical: No chemical treatment required
cultural: Maintain consistent drip irrigation and plastic or straw mulch

prevention: Monitor weekly with yellow sticky traps for thrips, aphids, and whiteflies
references: UC Davis Vegetable Research - Bell Pepper Production

Potato___Early_blight.description: Early blight of potato is caused by the fungus Alternaria solani. It targets mature foliage and tubers, producing characteristic target-board lesions with concentric rings.
symptoms: Circular to irregular dark brown lesions with concentric target rings
Narrow chlorotic yellow halos surrounding spots
Lesions start on older lower leaves and progress upward
Premature defoliation resulting in reduced tuber yield and tuber dry rot
causes: Fungus Alternaria solani
Overwintering in infected potato crop debris and solanaceous weeds
Alternating dry and wet conditions with temperatures around 24-29°C

organic: Copper octanoate or copper hydroxide preventive foliar spray
Bio-fungicides containing Bacillus amyloliquefaciens or Trichoderma
chemical: Mancozeb, Chlorothalonil, or Fluazinam as protectants
Azoxystrobin or Difenoconazole applied at early canopy closure
cultural: Maintain optimal plant nutrition; plants stressed for nitrogen or potassium are more susceptible
Avoid overhead irrigation, particularly late in the afternoon
Burn or deeply till under crop debris immediately following harvest

prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers
Practice 3 to 4 year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops
references: North Dakota State University Extension - Potato Early Blight
University of Idaho Extension - Potato Pathology

Potato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans (the pathogen of the Irish Potato Famine). It is an extraordinarily aggressive disease capable of destroying entire fields within days under cool, moist weather.
symptoms: Water-soaked dark green to black-brown lesions on leaves and stems
White, cottony downy fungal-like growth on the underside of lesions in humid conditions
Foul odor in heavily blighted fields as tissues decay
Tubers develop coppery brown granular rot under the skin
causes: Oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans
Survives exclusively in living host tissue (cull piles, volunteer potatoes, infected seed tubers)
Cool (15-20°C) and wet weather with relative humidity above 90%

organic: Bordeaux mixture or fixed copper fungicides applied before disease establishment
Immediate eradication and destruction of infected plants in organic setups
chemical: Cymoxanil, Mandipropamid, Fluopicolide, or Dimethomorph applied preventively
Metalaxyl / Mefenoxam (only where resistant strains are not prevalent)
cultural: Eliminate all potato cull piles by burying under at least 60 cm of soil or tarping
Destroy volunteer potato plants growing from previous seasons
Kill potato vines (flail or desiccant) 2 weeks before harvest to prevent tuber contamination

prevention: Plant certified late blight-free seed potatoes
Use disease forecasting tools (e.g., Blitecast) to time fungicide applications precisely
references: Cornell University - Late Blight Management Guide
International Potato Center (CIP) - Late Blight Protocols

Potato___healthy.description: Healthy potato plants exhibiting lush, dark green compound leaves, robust stems, full canopy vigor, and complete absence of blights, virus mosaics, or beetle feeding damage.
symptoms: Deep green pinnately compound leaves with vigorous expansion
Erect sturdy stems with healthy flowering clusters
No necrotic lesions, water-soaked margins, or curling

organic: Apply balanced potassium sulfate and organic compost tea drench
chemical: No chemical treatment required
cultural: Hill soil around stem bases to protect developing tubers from sun-greening

prevention: Scout regularly for Colorado potato beetle and potato leafhopper
Maintain uniform soil moisture during tuber bulking phase
references: University of Wisconsin Extension - Commercial Potato Production

Raspberry___healthy.description: Healthy red or black raspberry canes featuring vibrant green trifoliate or pentafoliate leaves, healthy canes, clean margins, and no symptoms of cane blight, spur blight, or rust.
symptoms: Uniform light to medium green leaves with white-felted undersides
Serrated margins without yellow borders or necrotic scorch
Healthy primocane and floricane shoot growth

organic: Maintain woodchip mulch and foliar micronutrient feeding
chemical: No chemical treatment required
cultural: Prune spent floricanes immediately after fruiting to improve sunlight penetration

prevention: Trellis canes to prevent ground contact and facilitate rapid wind drying
Plant in well-drained soils to prevent Phytophthora root rot
references: Cornell Berry Management - Raspberry Diagnostic Guide

Soybean___healthy.description: Healthy soybean plants showing uniform trifoliate leaves, rich green pigmentation, sturdy nodal development, and no symptoms of Frogeye leaf spot, soybean rust, or bacterial pustule.
symptoms: Uniform rich green trifoliate leaves
Intact leaf margins and healthy pubescence (fine hairs)
Normal node and pod development without premature chlorosis

organic: Ensure effective rhizobial inoculation at planting for atmospheric nitrogen fixation
chemical: No chemical treatment required
cultural: Maintain clean row cultivation and appropriate plant population

prevention: Rotate crops annually with non-legume crops (corn, sorghum, wheat)
Plant certified seeds treated with fungicide/insecticide seed treatments if soil is cold
references: Iowa State University Extension - Soybean Diseases Guide

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: Caused by Podosphaera xanthii (formerly Sphaerotheca fuliginea), powdery mildew affects all cucurbit crops, producing talcum powder-like fungal growth that leads to chlorosis and sunscalded fruit.
symptoms: White talcum powder-like circular patches on both upper and lower leaf surfaces
Patches expand rapidly, merging to cover the entire leaf blade and petiole
Infected leaves turn yellow, brown, and become dry and papery
Loss of protective foliage leads to fruit sunscald and reduced sugar content
causes: Fungus Podosphaera xanthii (Erysiphe cichoracearum)
Airborne conidia traveling long distances on wind currents
Warm dry weather (20-27°C) combined with dense canopy and low sunlight

organic: Potassium bicarbonate (MilStop) applied every 7-10 days
Horticultural oils (JMS Stylet-Oil) or neem oil sprays
Diluted milk whey spray (10-20% concentration) in bright sunlight
chemical: Quintec (Quinoxyfen), Torino (Cyflufenamid), or Vivando (Metrafenone)
Rotate with protectants such as Chlorothalonil or Sulfur
cultural: Prune dense outer foliage and space plants generously to maximize air passage
Avoid late-season overhead irrigation; use drip line watering

prevention: Select powdery mildew-resistant (PMR) squash and pumpkin cultivars
Start preventive spray programs early when first spots appear on crown leaves
references: Cornell University - Cucurbit Powdery Mildew Management
UC Davis IPM - Squash Powdery Mildew

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: Strawberry leaf scorch is caused by the ascomycete fungus Diplocarpon earlianum. It produces numerous purplish-red blotches that coalesce, causing the leaf margins to curl up and look scorched or burned.
symptoms: Small, irregular purplish to dark red spots without clear white centers (unlike leaf spot)
Spots enlarge and merge until entire leaf tissue turns purple then brown and dry
Leaf margins curl upward and dry out, giving a scorched or burned appearance
Infections extend to calyx (fruit cap), causing brown unmarketable fruit caps
causes: Fungus Diplocarpon earlianum
Overwintering in old infected leaves and runners
Extended leaf wetness (8-12+ hours) and warm temperatures (20-25°C)

organic: Copper hydroxide or liquid copper octanoate applied at early spring emergence
Bio-fungicides based on Bacillus subtilis
chemical: Captan 80 WDG or Thiram applied at pre-bloom and post-bloom intervals
Rally (Myclobutanil) or Switch (Cyprodinil + Fludioxonil)
cultural: Mow down and remove old foliage immediately after harvest renovation
Plant on raised beds with drip irrigation to keep foliage dry
Maintain weed-free beds to promote rapid dew drying

prevention: Plant certified disease-free strawberry runners
Select resistant cultivars (e.g., Allstar, Honeoye, Delite)
references: North Carolina State University Extension - Strawberry Leaf Scorch
Ohio State University Extension - Strawberry Foliar Diseases

Strawberry___healthy.description: Healthy strawberry plants displaying vibrant trifoliate leaves, rich green color, stout crowns, active runner development, and complete freedom from leaf spot, scorch, or Botrytis grey mold.
symptoms: Lush trifoliate green leaves with clean toothed margins
Sturdy crowns without rot or discoloration
Firm white flowers and healthy developing fruit caps (calyx)

organic: Apply balanced organic fish hydrolysate and kelp meal
chemical: No chemical treatment required
cultural: Maintain clean straw or plastic mulch under fruit to prevent soil contact

prevention: Monitor for two-spotted spider mites and strawberry aphids
Conduct post-harvest renovation to rejuvenate perennial beds
references: UC Davis IPM - Strawberry Production and Pest Management

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot is caused by four species of Xanthomonas (X. euvesicatoria, X. perforans, X. vesicatoria, X. gardneri). It causes small dark brown leaf lesions, defoliation, and fruit scabs.
symptoms: Small (less than 3mm), dark brown to black water-soaked circular leaf spots
Lesions develop a greasy or water-soaked appearance on leaf undersides
Severe leaf yellowing, browning, and premature defoliation
Small, raised, scab-like blister spots on tomato fruits
causes: Xanthomonas species complex bacteria
Infected seeds or transplants
Rain splash, high humidity, overhead irrigation, and temperatures between 24-30°C

organic: Fixed copper bactericide (Copper hydroxide) tank-mixed with Bacillus subtilis
Bacteriophage foliar spray (AgriPhage Tomato)
chemical: Copper hydroxide plus Mancozeb tank mix applied preventively
Actigard (Acibenzolar-S-methyl) systemic acquired resistance inducer
cultural: Strictly avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation beneath plastic mulch
Avoid entering or handling tomato plants while foliage is wet
Sanitize stakes, cages, and pruning equipment with 10% bleach or quaternary ammonium

prevention: Use certified pathogen-free, hot-water treated tomato seeds (50°C for 25 min)
Rotate crops with non-solanaceous species on a 2-3 year cycle
references: University of Florida IFAS - Tomato Bacterial Spot Management
Cornell University - Vegetable Pathology: Tomato Diseases

Tomato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is a common fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani. It produces distinct dark brown target-board lesions with concentric rings, primarily affecting older lower foliage first.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with concentric rings (target spot appearance)
Yellow chlorotic halos surrounding lesions
Starts on mature lower leaves and progresses upwards
Stem cankers near ground level in severe cases, causing collar rot
causes: Fungus Alternaria solani
Overwintering in solanaceous plant residue and weeds (nightshade)
Frequent heavy dew, rainfall, and warm temperatures (24-29°C)

organic: Apply cold-pressed neem oil spray (5ml per liter) every 7 days
Copper soap (Copper Octanoate) or Bordeaux mixture at first sign of spots
Bio-fungicide foliar drench using Bacillus subtilis
chemical: Mancozeb 75% WP (2-2.5 g/liter water)
Azoxystrobin 23% SC (1ml / liter) for translaminar control
Chlorothalonil 75% WP on alternate weeks
cultural: Stake and prune lower leaves (bottom 30 cm) to prevent ground splashback
Apply clean straw or plastic mulch to seal soil surface
Rotate solanaceous crops on a minimum 3-year cycle

prevention: Select tomato cultivars with high tolerance or resistance (e.g., Mountain Supreme, Defiant PhR)
Ensure wide plant spacing (60 cm) to facilitate quick canopy drying
references: Penn State Extension - Early Blight on Tomato
UC Davis IPM - Tomato Early Blight Guidelines

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Tomato late blight is caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans. It is an extremely destructive disease that rapidly destroys leaves, stems, and fruits during cool, wet weather.
symptoms: Large, irregular water-soaked pale-green to brown lesions on leaves
White fungal-like downy sporulation on the underside of leaves under humid conditions
Dark brown to black necrotic lesions on stems and petioles
Large, firm, greasy brown lesions on tomato fruits
causes: Oomycete pathogen Phytophthora infestans
Windblown sporangia from nearby infected potato or tomato crops
Cool (15-22°C), wet, foggy conditions with high relative humidity (>90%)

organic: Copper hydroxide or Bordeaux mixture applied thoroughly before rain events
Immediate eradication and bagging of heavily infected vines to prevent field epidemic
chemical: Mandipropamid (Revus), Cymoxanil (Curzate), or Dimethomorph
Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb as protective barrier sprays
cultural: Plant in full sun with maximum airflow
Avoid overhead irrigation; use base drip irrigation only
Destroy volunteer tomato and potato plants in and around the farm

prevention: Plant late blight-resistant tomato varieties (e.g., Mountain Magic, Defiant PhR, Plum Regal)
Track local extension disease alerts and forecast indices (USABlight)
references: Cornell University - Late Blight of Tomato and Potato
USABlight - National Late Blight Reporting Network

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: Tomato leaf mold is caused by the fungus Passalora fulva (formerly Cladosporium fulvum). It is predominantly a high-tunnel and greenhouse problem, thriving under high relative humidity.
symptoms: Pale green to yellowish chlorotic patches on the upper surface of older leaves
Dense, olive-green to grayish velvety fungal mold on corresponding leaf undersides
Infected leaves curl, wither, and drop prematurely
Blossom blighting and reduced fruit set
causes: Fungus Passalora fulva (Cladosporium fulvum)
Overwintering in greenhouse wooden structures, tools, and crop residue
Relative humidity consistently above 85% with temperatures around 21-24°C

organic: Bio-fungicides based on Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma
Copper-based fungicides applied to thorough leaf underside coverage
chemical: Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb protectant sprays
Difenoconazole + Cyprodinil (Inspire Super) for systemic curative control
cultural: Aggressively ventilate greenhouses using exhaust fans, ridge vents, and horizontal airflow fans
Heat and vent simultaneously in evening to lower relative humidity below 80%
Prune lower suckers and dense canopy leaves to improve air passage

prevention: Select resistant tomato varieties carrying Cf-resistance genes
Sanitize greenhouse interiors between cropping cycles using sanitizers
references: University of Massachusetts Extension - Tomato Leaf Mold Management
Ohio State University - Greenhouse Tomato Diseases

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: Septoria leaf spot is caused by the fungus Septoria lycopersici. It is characterized by numerous small, circular spots with dark brown margins and gray centers containing tiny black specks.
symptoms: Numerous small (1.5 to 3 mm), circular spots with dark brown margins and ash-gray centers
Tiny black pimple-like pycnidia fruiting bodies visible inside gray centers with hand lens
Leaves turn completely yellow, wither, and drop off starting from the base upward
Fruit is rarely infected directly, but defoliation leads to severe sunscald
causes: Fungus Septoria lycopersici
Overwintering in solanaceous plant debris and weed hosts (horsenettle)
Prolonged leaf wetness and warm temperatures (20-25°C) with rain splash dispersal

organic: Liquid copper octanoate or copper sulfate applied at first appearance
Serenade Garden (Bacillus subtilis) foliar wash
chemical: Chlorothalonil (Daconil) applied on a 7-10 day schedule
Mancozeb or Quadris (Azoxystrobin) in rotation
cultural: Strip off lower 2-3 sets of leaves once plants reach 1 meter tall
Apply a 5-8 cm organic mulch barrier beneath plants to stop soil splash
Avoid working in tomato beds when leaves are wet

prevention: Perform a 3-year crop rotation out of solanaceous crops
Till under or incinerate all tomato residues immediately following final harvest
references: Missouri Botanical Garden - Septoria Leaf Spot of Tomato
Purdue Extension - Septoria Leaf Spot Management

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Damage caused by the pest Tetranychus urticae (Two-spotted spider mite). These microscopic arachnids pierce plant cell walls and suck out contents, causing severe stippling, bronzing, and silky webbing.
symptoms: Fine white to yellow stippling (tiny dots) on the upper leaf surface
Leaves take on a bronzed, dusty, or scorched appearance
Silky, fine webbing visible on leaf undersides and shoot tips
Severe leaf curling, desiccation, and premature leaf drop
causes: Two-spotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae)
Hot, dry, dusty environmental conditions (temperatures above 30°C with low humidity)
Overuse of broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroid insecticides that destroy natural predatory mites

organic: Apply Insecticidal Soap or Potassium Salts of Fatty Acids covering undersides
Neem oil (Azadirachtin) or pure cold-pressed horticultural mineral oils
Release biological predatory mites: Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus
chemical: Bifenazate (Acramite) or Spiromesifen (Oberon) miticides
Abamectin (Agri-Mek) for translaminar mite knockdown
Rotate chemical classes to prevent rapid miticide resistance development
cultural: Mist or hose down dusty road margins to minimize dust drift onto fields
Overhead spray washing of leaf undersides on home garden plants
Remove and bag heavily infested isolated plants before mites spread via webbing

prevention: Preserve natural predators (lady beetles, lacewings, predatory mites)
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization which produces succulent foliage preferred by mites
references: UC Davis IPM - Spider Mites on Tomato
University of Florida IFAS - Two-spotted Spider Mite Management

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: Target spot is caused by the fungal pathogen Corynespora cassiicola. It causes brown circular lesions with concentric rings and can defoliate plants and cause sunken lesions on fruit.
symptoms: Small water-soaked pinpoint spots that enlarge into circular brown lesions
Prominent concentric rings resembling a target board with a light-tan center
Chlorotic yellow halo surrounding the lesion margin
Deep, sunken dark lesions on tomato fruit shoulders
causes: Fungus Corynespora cassiicola
Survival on solanaceous and cucurbit crop residue
Warm temperatures (20-28°C) and high humidity or prolonged rainfall

organic: Copper hydroxide or basic copper sulfate applied preventively
Bacillus amyloliquefaciens bio-fungicide sprays
chemical: Fluopyram + Trifloxystrobin (Luna Sensation) or Pyraclostrobin + Boscalid (Cabrio)
Chlorothalonil or Mancozeb as contact protectants
cultural: Improve canopy airflow through vertical staking and sucker pruning
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation exclusively
Deep-plow or destroy crop residues after harvest

prevention: Rotate crops away from tomatoes, peppers, and cucurbits for at least 2 seasons
Ensure adequate in-row plant spacing to prevent dense, trapped moisture
references: University of Florida IFAS Extension - Target Spot of Tomato
Mississippi State University Extension - Tomato Target Spot Management

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) is a begomovirus transmitted by the sweetpotato whitefly (Bemisia tabaci). It causes severe stunting, upward leaf curling, chlorosis, and total flower drop.
symptoms: Severe upward curling and cupping of leaflets
Interveinal chlorosis and yellowing of leaf margins
Marked reduction in leaf size (leaves appear small and bunched)
Severe plant stunting with an erect, bushy appearance and failure to set fruit
causes: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Begomovirus (TYLCV)
Vectored persistently by the whitefly Bemisia tabaci
Not seed-transmitted; relies entirely on insect vectors or infected vegetative transplants

organic: Spray insecticidal soap or horticultural oil to smother whitefly nymphs
Release biological control agents such as Encarsia formosa parasitic wasps
Apply reflective silver plastic mulches to disorient incoming whiteflies
chemical: Systemic neonicotinoids (Imidacloprid, Dinotefuran) or Cyantraniliprole to suppress whiteflies
Pyriproxyfen or Buprofezin insect growth regulators to halt nymphal development
No chemical cures the virus once the plant is infected; infected plants must be rogued
cultural: Rogue (pull up and destroy) symptomatic plants immediately, placed in sealed bags
Maintain a 6-week tomato-free host crop break before planting season
Eradicate weed hosts such as nightshades, cheeseweed, and jimsonweed

prevention: Plant resistant/tolerant tomato cultivars carrying Ty-1, Ty-2, or Ty-3 resistance genes
Install insect-proof exclusion netting (50-mesh) on nursery structures and greenhouses
references: UC Davis IPM - Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus
University of Florida IFAS - TYLCV Management Guide

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV) is a highly stable tobamovirus. It causes mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns on leaves, fern-like leaf distortion, internal fruit browning, and reduced vigor.
symptoms: Mottling with alternating light green and dark green mosaic patterns on leaves
Distortion of leaf shape: blistering, puckering, and narrow 'shoestring' or fern-like leaves
Stunting of the whole plant with bronzed or brown necrotic streaks on stems
Internal brown corky ring necrosis in fruit tissue
causes: Tomato Mosaic Tobamovirus (ToMV)
Mechanically transmitted via contaminated hands, tools, pruning shears, and clothing
Seed transmission via contaminated seed coat
Extremely durable; can persist in root debris, tools, and tobacco products for years

organic: Spray non-fat dry milk solution (20%) during pruning to deactivate virus on hands and blades
No organic curative spray exists once infected; remove and burn infected plants
chemical: No antiviral chemical pesticides exist for plant viruses
Sanitize tools with Virkon-S, Trisodium Phosphate (TSP 10%), or household bleach
cultural: Workers should wash hands thoroughly with soap and avoid using tobacco products near plants
Rogue out and incinerate infected plants immediately without touching healthy neighbors
Clean and heat-sterilize stakes, wire trellises, and potting trays between crops

prevention: Plant resistant tomato hybrids carrying Tm-2 or Tm-2^2 resistance genes
Use certified virus-free seeds treated with heat (70°C for 3 days) or 10% TSP
references: Penn State Extension - Tomato Mosaic Virus (ToMV)
University of Minnesota Extension - Mosaic Viruses on Tomato

Tomato___healthy.description: Healthy tomato foliage characterized by rich green pinnate leaves, robust glandular trichomes (leaf hairs), upright stems, and total absence of bacterial specks, fungal blights, or viral mosaics.
symptoms: Deep green leaves with uniform chlorophyll distribution
Clean leaf margins without chlorosis, necroses, or curled margins
Sturdy central stem with healthy flower truss development

organic: Apply balanced seaweed extract bio-stimulants and compost tea root drenches
chemical: No chemical intervention required
cultural: Maintain regular drip irrigation scheduling and supportive vertical trellising

prevention: Monitor weekly using sticky traps for preventive pest scouting
Prune bottom foliage touching the soil surface to maintain hygiene
references: USDA Agricultural Research Service - Tomato Health Protocols
Cornell Vegetable Program - Tomato Production Guidelines
